idiom_name: closure stored by the context (protocol existential for heterogeneous, stateful strategies)
implementation_notes: Closures are Swift's strategy value: the context stores a (Double) -> Double or receives it as a parameter, marked @escaping when it is retained, and the standard library takes comparison strategies exactly this way in sorted(by:)/sort(by:). For strategies that carry state, group several operations, or must be chosen from a heterogeneous set, declare a protocol and hold it as an existential (any PricingStrategy) - the protocol witness table is Swift's vtable - or take it as a generic parameter (some PricingStrategy) to keep static dispatch and avoid boxing. Foundation's SortComparator/Sequence.sorted(using:) shows the protocol-based form designed for composition. Closures capture strongly, so a strategy stored on the object it captures needs an explicit capture list.
pitfalls: A stored closure that captures the context creates a retain cycle (context -> closure -> context); use a capture list ([weak self] / [unowned self]) or a stateless strategy value.
A closure passed to an initializer that stores it must be @escaping; adding it where the closure is only called synchronously documents the wrong lifetime (and vice versa fails to compile).
Any-protocol existentials box values and dispatch through a witness table; a generic parameter or some/opaque type keeps static dispatch, so do not default to any for hot-path strategies.
